# Would the dropped hammer hit the right-hand propeller?

**Short answer: No — it would miss, though only just.** If the workman opened his
hand and let the hammer fall, it would drop through the open wedge of sky between
him and the propeller, pass a few centimetres clear of the leading edge of the
nearest blade's lower tip, and land on *him* — on his own raised, bent knee — and
then onto the box and the heavy timber staging at his feet. It would not land on
the propeller. At most, a tumbling hammer might graze the extreme tip of that one
blade on the way past.

## What is in the picture

A twin-screw ship is in dry dock, photographed from below and behind the stern, so
the camera is pitched steeply upwards (the distant shoreline sits about 86 % of the
way down the frame instead of halfway). The big propeller filling the left half of
the picture is a four-bladed screw and is the nearer of the two. The right-hand
propeller is the more distant one: its shaft comes out of the hull at the upper
right, its boss and rope guard sit up and to the right of the man, one blade
sweeps up and to the left, one runs off the right edge of the frame, and one
sweeps down and to the left, ending in a rounded tip right beside him at about
knee height.

The man stands on a heavy timber between the two propellers, facing right. One leg
is straight; the other is bent with the knee raised and the foot up on a dark box.
His right arm is raised and he holds a hammer head-uppermost, handle sloping down
to his fist — he is mid-swing at whatever he is chipping or sounding on the blade.

## Where the hammer actually is

Measured on the image (458 × 480 pixels):

- The hammer head is a dark blob spanning about x = 307–316, y = 287–291, centred
  near (311, 289). His fist is at about (321, 308). The hammer's centre of mass,
  which is what governs a free fall, sits close to the head at roughly (312, 291).
- At that same height the nearest edge of the right propeller's blade is at about
  x = 345 — some 30 pixels away, roughly 35 cm at his scale. **The hammer is not
  being held over the propeller at all.** It is held over the bright empty gap
  between the man and the blade, and for the first 100 pixels of its fall there is
  nothing beneath it but sky.
- The blade slants down and to the left as it descends: its left edge is at
  x ≈ 330 at y = 324, x ≈ 323 at y = 360, and it reaches its leftmost point of
  x ≈ 315 at y ≈ 387 before the rounded tip closes off at about (320, 403).

## Tracing the fall

Because the camera is tilted upwards, true world verticals are not exactly
vertical in the picture — they splay outwards from the frame's centre line as they
descend. I calibrated this on a thin vertical pole in the distant dockyard
background near x = 406: its dark centroid drifts from x ≈ 405.7 at y = 344 to
x ≈ 407.7 at y = 375, a slope of about +0.065 px sideways per px of descent at that
distance from the centre. Scaled to the hammer's position, a falling object
starting near x = 312 drifts right by only about 0.03 px per px of fall.

The resulting fall line:

- **y = 308** — x ≈ 312.5. It skims past the peak of his cap, whose visor reaches
  x ≈ 311 at exactly that height. It very nearly clips his own head on the way
  down.
- **y = 387–403** — x ≈ 315.4–315.9. This is the decisive stretch. The blade's
  leftmost edge here is x ≈ 315 rising to 318. The hammer therefore skims straight
  down the narrow white sliver of sky between the man and the blade's leading
  edge, passing outside it by only a couple of pixels — a few centimetres in real
  terms.
- **y = 402–416** — x ≈ 315.9–316.3. This is squarely inside the dark mass of his
  raised bent knee, which spans roughly x = 300–322 at that height and is clearly
  lifted (there is a strip of light beneath it, so it is a raised leg, not a box).
  This is what the hammer actually lands on.
- Below that it would bounce or roll onto the box (about x = 316–334,
  y = 415–441) and the timber he is standing on.

## The depth question, and how close the call really is

Whether the two objects collide depends on depth as well as left–right position,
so I checked that too. Fitting the left propeller's visible blade tips gives a
projected disc with conjugate semi-radii of about 142 and 185 pixels, i.e. a disc
tilted roughly 40° out of the picture plane. The right propeller images
correspondingly smaller, consistent with it being roughly 1.3 times farther from
the camera. Working back through the man's apparent height (about 144 px for a
1.7 m man), the man sits in depth between the two screws, about a metre in front
of the right propeller's disc centre — and the down-left blade happens to lie
close to the disc's foreshortened axis, so its tip is thrown about the same
distance towards the camera. **In other words, the blade tip and the man are at
essentially the same depth**, which is exactly why he can stand there and work on
it. Depth therefore neither saves the hammer nor condemns it; the answer really is
decided by the left–right geometry above.

I should be straightforward about the margin. The clearance at the critical point
is only about two to four pixels, which is comparable to the size of the hammer
head itself and to my own uncertainty in locating its centre of mass. Dropping
from the fist rather than the head would put the line inside the blade; dropping
from the head puts it outside. And a real dropped hammer tumbles, sweeping a band
wider than a single point. So this is a near-miss rather than a comfortable one.

## Conclusion

No — the hammer would not hit the right propeller. The propeller is off to his
right, not above his feet: the boss, the rope guard, the upper blade and the whole
body of the down-swept blade are all well up and to the right of the line of fall.
The only part of the propeller in contention is the very tip of one blade, and the
hammer passes just to the left of it. The hammer would come down on the man's own
raised knee and then onto the box and staging at his feet. The worst the propeller

**No. If the old man let go of the hammer, it would not hit the right propeller. It would fall onto his own raised arm and then down to the ground in front of him, passing just to the left of the propeller's lower blade tip.**

## What the picture shows

The photograph is taken from low down under the stern of a ship in dry dock. Two large propellers hang below the hull: a big one on the left and a smaller-looking one on the right. An older workman in a flat cap and overalls stands on heavy timber planks on the dock floor between them, facing to the right toward the right-hand propeller. His arm is raised and he holds a hammer cocked back over his head, roughly level with the right propeller's hub but well to the left of it. The right propeller's lower blade sweeps down from the hub toward the man and ends in a rounded tip at about his knee height, a little in front of his legs.

## Tracing a straight vertical drop from the hammer

1. **The hammer is above the man, not above the propeller.** The hammer head sits above and slightly in front of the man's face. The propeller hub and the roots of the blades are clearly further to the right of the hammer, so no part of the hub or upper blade lies under it.

2. **First thing below the hammer: his own arm.** Directly beneath the hammer head, about 30 cm down, is the man's raised forearm and elbow. A dropped hammer would land on his arm first.

3. **Then the gap in front of his body.** Below the arm, the drop line runs down the narrow strip of open sky between the front of the man's body and the leading edge of the propeller blade. That edge slants from the hub (upper right) down toward the blade tip (lower left) and stays to the right of the drop line the whole way.

4. **At the bottom: the ground, not the blade tip.** The drop line reaches the level of the blade tip just to the left of the tip. Measured on the 458-pixel-wide image, the hammer head is centred at about x=311, while the lit left edge of the blade tip begins at about x=314-315 and the main gray blade surface at about x=316-317. So the centre of the hammer's fall line clears the tip by a few pixels, which at this scale is only a few centimetres. Below the tip the line meets a dark rounded object (a separate item sitting behind the blade, not part of the propeller) and then the dark block and planks at the man's feet.

5. **Depth makes the miss more certain.** The camera is well off the propeller shaft axis (the left propeller appears about 1.4 times larger than the right one, and the hubs are seen as side-on cylinders), so the propeller discs are viewed obliquely. That means the lower blade tip, which is displaced sideways from the hub, sits at a different distance from the camera than the hub the man is working at. In three dimensions the tip is therefore very likely not even in the same vertical plane as the hammer, even though it looks close in the flat image.

## Conclusion

The hammer would hit the man's own arm and then the ground beside the propeller. It would pass just to the left of the lower blade tip of the right propeller. At the very most, the outer end of the hammer head might brush the extreme edge of that blade tip, but it would not strike the propeller's hub or blade surfaces. So the answer is no, it would not hit the right propeller; it would narrowly miss it.

Note on interpretation: if "drop the hammer down" is meant as "swing the hammer down", then yes, he is obviously poised to strike the root of the right propeller's blade directly in front of his hand, since that is the work he is doing. But for a hammer simply released and falling under gravity, the answer is no.

# Answer: No — the dropped hammer would miss the right propeller

**The answer is No.** If the old man let go of the hammer and it fell straight down, it would not hit the propeller on the right side of the image. It would fall through the gap of sky to the left of that propeller's lower blade and land on the staging below.

## What each thing is, stated explicitly

- The “right propeller” means the propeller on the right side of the photograph as viewed. Its hub and shaft are on the right edge of the image and its lower blade hangs down to the right of the man.
- The “old man” is the workman standing on the wooden blocks in the centre-right of the image, facing right with his right arm raised.
- The “hammer” is the small T-shaped tool in his raised right hand. Its head is above his hand and slightly to the left of his hand because the handle slopes down to the right.

## Why straight down means straight down in the image

- A dropped object falls vertically in the world.
- The camera looks horizontally and appears level, so world-vertical is image-vertical. Cropping and enlarging the region around the man and the right blade confirms that a world-vertical fall is a vertical line in the picture. No perspective correction changes left versus right here.

## Where the hammer is relative to the blade

- At the hammer’s height there is open sky between the man’s hand and the propeller. The hammer head, centred near x = 311 in the 458-pixel-wide original, sits well to the left of the propeller cone tip and well to the left of the upper part of the lower blade, whose left edge at that height is near x = 335.
- Enlarged crops show the head as a small dark bar against sky, with its centroid at about x = 311.3. The handle runs down to the right to about x = 316–317 where it meets the hand. The hand itself, which is flesh and not part of the falling hammer’s metal, extends farther right to about x = 323–326.
- Tracing the blade’s left edge down, it moves left as the blade widens toward its tip, but it stays to the right of the hammer head all the way down. Subpixel measurement of the sky-to-blade transition gives a left edge near x = 334.8 at upper levels, near x = 322.6 at mid-blade, near x = 318.5 higher down, and nearest about x = 314.6–315.0 just above the tip. The hammer head at x = 311.3 is therefore about 3–4 pixels left of the blade at its closest approach. In the original scale that is a small but real daylight gap, visible in the enlargements as sky directly below the head.
- The blade tip itself is at about the same x as the hammer head, but lower down where the hammer head will never be at the same time as the tip unless the whole hammer is considered. The only near-contact in projection is the butt end of the handle grazing the extreme left edge by about one to two pixels after a long fall, which is within blur and edge softness and still left of the blade face. The head, which is the part meant by “the hammer” falling from where it is, clearly passes left of the metal.

## What would happen

- Released gently with no throw, the hammer would keep its orientation briefly and fall straight down. Its head would travel down the sky gap. It would pass to the left of the blade face and to the left of the blade tip.
- It would therefore not strike the right propeller. It would continue past the tip level and fall to the wooden block and ground near the man’s feet, between the man and the propeller.
- Rotation as a head-heavy object falls would, if anything, swing the head slightly farther left, away from the blade, so it does not turn a miss into a hit.

## Conclusion restated explicitly

- The hammer starts to the left of the right propeller in the image.
- Its vertical path stays to the left of the right propeller’s blade.
- So dropping it would not make it hit the right propeller. The answer is No, it would miss just to the left of the blade.
